title: Preemptive Reservoir: Tiered, Stateful Load‑Shedding with Partial‑Response Fallbacks
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Background:
We currently use tiered priority lanes and token-bucket admission for handling overload, but customer traffic patterns with spiky multi-region failovers show two gaps: (1) sudden cross-region spill causes localized queues to back up and token buckets to exhaust without graceful partial delivery, and (2) model-variant fallbacks and quantized pathways are not coordinated with admission, resulting in quality cliffs.

Proposal summary:
Implement a Preemptive Reservoir admission controller: a small, stateful reservoir per host (with optional per-tenant accounting) that proactively preempts lower-priority queued requests when pressure hits threshold X. The reservoir supports staged degradation modes: (A) partial-response streaming (early tokens + warning), (B) model-slimming fallback (lower-precision/shorter decode), and (C) reject-with-grace (HTTP 429 + retry-after + suggested route). Admission decisions are informed by a short-lived quality sampler and a region-aware spill handler which negotiates capacity credits across regions in the event of failover.

Goals and success metrics:
- Maintain 99th-percentile tail latency SLOs for P0 and P1 tenants during regional failover spikes.
- Reduce downstream error propagation by 50% when load-shedding engages (measured via error-rate on downstream retries).
- Preserve end-to-end perceived quality: mean quality drop (measured against prompt-level evals) < 10% for P0 tenants when using model-slimming fallback.

Design details:
1) Reservoir semantics:
   - Capacity: small fixed buffer (configurable per host and tenant slice).
   - Tokens: admission credits consumed per-request based on estimated tokens (model, sequence length histogram).
   - Preemption: when reservoir full, eviction favors preemptive drop of lowest-priority queued items using LRU + priority decay (recent heavy tenants get slight priority aging to avoid starvation).

2) Degradation ladder (policy ordered):
   - Ladder 0 (Preferred): accept on full pathway.
   - Ladder 1 (Partial‑response streaming): return first N tokens synchronously, mark response as partial and schedule async completion (if credits free later).
   - Ladder 2 (Model‑slim fallback): switch to quantized or shorter‑context model variant with adjusted sampling to preserve coherence.
   - Ladder 3 (Graceful reject): return structured 429 with metadata: reason, retry-after, alternate endpoints, and an immediate short-lived trial token if available.

3) Multi‑region spill handler:
   - Each region emits capacity credits to global control plane with conservative staleness TTL.
   - On neighbor-region failover, receiving region can request credits; source region provides limited burst credit up to a configured share.
   - If credit negotiation fails, reservoir preemption thresholds tighten progressively.

4) Circuit breaker integration:
   - Circuit breakers use a sampled quality metric (rolling 30s window) and a latency window. When quality drops AND latency rises above SLO, breakers force ladder 2 or 3 automatically for affected tenant classes.

Runtime/Implementation notes:
- Admission controller implemented as a pluggable module in the serving runtime (C++/Rust runtime component).
- Lightweight per-host in-memory state, durable to local crash via periodic snapshots to Redis for cross-host rehydration (snapshotting is small: reservoir token counts + per-tenant short history).
- Control-plane policies (reservoir size, ladder thresholds, inter-region credit limits) are pushed via Console and stored in ConfigStore.

API changes / telemetry:
- New response header X-Redwood-Shedding-Ladder: 0|1|2|3 and X-Redwood-Shedding-TokenUse.
- Console dashboard tile: Reservoir fill, preemptions/sec, ladder distribution, inter-region credit usage.
- Alerting rules: preemptions/sec spike, ladder-2-percentage > 20% for more than 2m for P0 tenants.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for reservoir eviction policy and per-tenant accounting.
- Integration tests with multi-region failover simulator (inject region outage and verify credit negotiation).
- Chaos job that introduces aggressive spike to validate preemption and ladder transitions without violating P0 SLO in 90% of runs.
- Quality regression harness: run representative prompt set across ladder 1/2 to verify mean quality drop < 10%.

Rollout plan:
- Canary (runtime-1.21-canary): enable reservoir in read-only measurement mode (no preemptions) across 5% of hosts. Validate metrics and quality sampler. (1 week)
- Soft enable: enable preemption for internal tenants only and run for 48 hours. (1 week)
- Customer gradual rollout: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback gates at each step (monitor SLOs, preemption impact).

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end test suite passes in CI with reservoir enabled.
- Canary telemetry shows stable reservoir metrics and quality sampler < 5% false positives.
- On controlled spike, P0 99p latency remains within 1.2x baseline in 90th percentile of runs.

Trade-offs and alternatives considered:
- Centralized global queue: considered but rejected due to cross-region latency and single-point-of-failure.
- Pure probabilistic shedding: simpler to implement but causes unpredictable quality cliffs; reservoir provides bounded guarantees.
- Full async fallback (always complete asynchronously): increases tail work and complicates charging; we prefer staged partial responses for latency-sensitive tenants.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Tenant billing and observability for partial responses: do we bill full token cost on staged completions or prorate? (Product decision).
- How aggressive should inter-region credit lending be for enterprise customers with reserved capacity? (Sales/PM input).
- KMS/HSM and audit logging needs for control-plane snapshots (security to advise).

- Multi-region simulator harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/failover-sim
